# Introducing Olmo-core 3: Open, scalable training infrastructure for large MoEs 

Published October 1, 2026 

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms 

Today we’re releasing Olmo-core 3, a significant upgrade to our framework for developing large language models featuring a redesigned open mixture-of-experts (MoE) training system.

Olmo-core 3 is designed to scale MoE training into the trillion-parameter range while preserving computational efficiency. It’s one of the core systems behind the next generation of Olmo, and part of our ongoing commitment to open up the tools and training infrastructure behind each new model.
...
Olmo-core 3 is built to close that gap. In one benchmark, we increased the expert pool from 8 to 128 while still selecting only four experts per token – the small units of text a language model processes – keeping the number of active parameters per token roughly fixed at about 3.2B. Total parameter capacity grew from 4.6B to 47B, while training throughput fell by less than 5%.

The same infrastructure has been benchmarked at over one trillion total parameters.

Our earlier MoE implementation in Olmo-core used fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), configured to gather and reshard model weights for each small batch of training data. Olmo-core 3 switches to a system based on distributed data parallelism (DDP). It keeps experts resident on GPUs and routes the relevant data to them, avoiding that repeated weight gathering.

NVIDIA’s Megatron-Core is an established option for training large MoEs. Olmo-core 3 brings an integrated MoE training stack to the framework behind Olmo, with a redesign that improves throughput over our earlier FSDP-based implementation. In a preliminary test on eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs, a 47-billion-parameter MoE processed 52,000 tokens per second per GPU with the new stack, compared with 19,400 using our earlier implementation—about 2.7× the throughput.

Olmo-core 3 also reduces the cost of routing data to the right experts and running their computations. Rowwise expert parallelism places routed data directly into expert input buffers, minimizing the extra work needed to rearrange it. GPU-resident routing keeps routing metadata on the GPUs, so the CPU can queue work without waiting for that information to be copied back. signals.excerpt:
Helion GEMM Backend Beats vLLM Defaults on Hopper

 Technology 03 October 2026 

# PyTorch Helion GEMM Backend Beats vLLM's Default Kernels on Hopper in Team Benchmarks

PyTorch researchers built a Helion linear backend for a vLLM fork, reporting 1.11× to 1.18× GEMM speedups on Hopper. It turns GEMM variant selection into a tunable parameter instead of hand-written dispatch heuristics.

 Helion
...
PyTorch-native ... hardware-agnostic
...
PyTorch researchers integrated Helion into vLLM's linear backend to test whether an autotuned, high-level kernel DSL can raise LLM inference performance while cutting kernel implementation complexity. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, the Helion backend pairs per-shape tuning with hybrid dispatch. Per the team's benchmarks, it beats vLLM's default CUTLASS and DeepGEMM backends across the evaluated models, with more than 10% throughput improvement for some workloads.

The work integrates Helion into vLLM's linear backend, with contributors from the OCTO and vLLM teams at Red Hat and the Helion team at Meta. The implementation lives in a vLLM fork rather than the upstream project, and the authors are still exploring how it would be maintained if adopted more broadly.

Helion is a PyTorch-native, hardware-agnostic ... DSL built around a tile-programming model. A developer writes a kernel once in Pythonic code, and Hel ... generates specialized versions for different workloads and hardware. Instead of hand-tuning each variant, Helion's ahead-of-time autotuner explores a defined search space — from memory layout and scheduling up to algorithmic choices — and picks the best-performing configuration. It also supports LLM-guided search to speed up tuning.

That abstraction matters for general matrix multiplication (GEMM), the core operation of quantized linear layers. Traditionally, kernel authors implement several algorithmic variants, benchmark them, and write dispatch heuristics. The variants include Standard GEMM, Split-K (which partitions the K dimension across thread blocks when M or N is small) and Swap-AB (which rewrites A@B as ([email protected]).T to help shapes with a small M dimension). vLLM's current Block_FP8 backend, for example, switches to Swap-AB when M < 32 on Hopper.

With Helion, a single implementation covers all three variants. The algorithmic choices become tunable parameters — in the sample kernel, split_k is constrained to powers of two up to 256 and swap_ab is a Boolean — and the autotuner selects the variant and low-level config per workload. The quantized GEMM kernels used in the work follow the same structure with added quantization and scaling logic.

The backend targets NVIDIA Hopper GPUs using Helion's Triton backend, covering three quantization formats: FP8_Dynamic (FP8 per-token activation, per-channel weight scaling), W8A8_INT8 (INT8 with per-token activation and per-channel weight scaling), and Block_FP8 (FP8 with 1×128 activation scaling and 128×128 weight scaling). Initial results with Helion's CuteDSL backend show competitive GEMM performance on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, and the authors say the work can extend to Blackwell as that backend matures.

A hybrid dispatch strategy keeps Helion's costs in check. For shapes up to max_helion_size — set to 32 for this work — the backend dispatches to Helion under CUDA Graph replay; larger shapes fall back to CUTLASS or DeepGEMM. The authors say this eliminates Helion's runtime CPU overhead from kernel dispatch and launch. It also narrows tuning to the small num_tokens range that dominates decoding, and shrinks the set of pre-tuned configs that must be validated and shipped.

Autotuning runs per input shape. With max_helion_size = 32, vLLM captures CUDA Graphs at [1, 2, 4] + range(8, 256, 8) + range(256, max_graph_size + 1, 16), and the Helion kernels are tuned for num_tokens = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32]. Benchmarking runs with CUDA Graphs enabled to match real inference conditions. Configs were generated with the LLMSeededLFBOTreeSearch autotuner, which uses an LLM — Claude Opus 4.8 for this work — to seed promising candidates for the subsequent tree search.

All benchmarks ran on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPU across six models: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, and the newer Qwen3.8-27B. Each was tested in three 8-bit quantization formats. At the kernel level, the PyTorch/Red Hat/Meta authors report that for FP8_Dynamic Helion posted a geometric mean speedup of 1.110× over CUTLASS, and for W8A8_INT8 it posted 1.178× over CUTLASS. For Block_FP8, they report it posted 1.149× over FlashInfer and 1.177× over DeepGEMM. The distribution varies across individual shapes, which the authors present as evidence for per-shape tuning over a single generic config.

End-to-end serving tests used ShareGPT prompts with --max-num-seqs 32, tensor parallel size 1, and prefix caching disabled, comparing the Helion backend against CutlassFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel, CutlassInt8ScaledMMLinearKernel, and FlashInferFp8DeepGEMMDynamicBlockScaledKernel. Across the evaluated models and formats, the team reports consistent end-to-end gains, with throughput improvement exceeding 10% for some workloads.
...
- A Helion linear backend was integrated into a vLLM fork, targeting quantized GEMM on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs with Helion's Triton backend.
- One Helion GEMM implementation covers Standard GEMM, Split-K, and Swap-AB as tunable parameters, with per-shape autotuning selecting variant and config.
- Kernel-level geometric mean speedups reported by the PyTorch/Red Hat/Meta authors: 1.110× FP8_Dynamic over CUTLASS, 1.178× W8A8_INT8 over CUTLASS, 1.149× Block_FP8 over FlashInfer, 1.177× Block_FP8 over DeepGEMM.
- End-to-end tests on an NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 across six Qwen3/Qwen3.8 models show consistent gains, with more than 10% throughput improvement for some workloads, per the authors.
- Hybrid dispatch uses Helion under CUDA Graph replay up to max_helion_size = 32 num_tokens, falling back to CUTLASS/DeepGEMM beyond that.
...
The most interesting claim here is not the speedup — roughly 1.1× to 1.18× at the kernel level is meaningful but incremental. It is that algorithmic variant selection stopped being a hand-written heuristic and became a tunable parameter. That said, the results are vendor-reported on one GPU class with configs generated using a specific LLM-seeded autotuner, and the deployment model the authors propose pushes tuning cost onto end users. Whether that trade holds for serving providers is the open question.

signals.excerpt:
In this blog post, we present our work on Jagged Flash Attention (JFA) — the attention kernel behind Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) — on NVIDIA Blackwell (B200), built with TLX (Triton Low-level Extensions), which add explicit, hardware-aware control on top of Triton’s high-level, tile-based programming model. 

Attention is the single slowest kernel in GEM, and reaching peak Blackwell performance has traditionally required hand-written CuteDSL or CUDA — slow to develop and hard to extend to new variants. We show that TLX closes this gap on both fronts. On development efficiency, the TLX attention kernel is about 3.2K lines of concise Triton-level code — roughly 3× less than the ~10K-line CuteDSL kernels of the state-of-the-art FlashAttention-4 (FA4). On performance, it outperforms FA4 (May 2026 version)  on the jagged shapes that matter for GEM — by ~13% on the forward pass and ~50% on the backward pass. And by staying in Triton’s high-level model, the kernel is approachable enough for modeling engineers, not just kernel specialists, to read, extend, and fuse.

We organize the work in two parts — the structural changes the TLX rewrite makes possible, and the optimizations we layer on top — all benchmarked in bfloat16 on B200 against FA4, the current state of the art on Blackwell.
...
Warp specialization, explicit shared-/tensor-memory management, and barrier pipelining are standard ingredients of any high-performance Blackwell attention kernel, so we keep this brief — what matters is that TLX lets us express them in high-level Triton code rather than hand-written CuteDSL or CUDA, which is what made the §2.2 optimizations fast to prototype. Concretely, we split the CTA into role-specialized async tasks — dedicated warps for TMA loads, tensor-core matmuls, softmax/correction math, and the epilogue store, plus a dedicated dQ-reduction warp in the backward — so the tensor cores stay fed with back-to-back MMAs while softmax runs concurrently, instead of one warp group stalling the matmuls as in the baseline.
...
explicit control extends to memory and scheduling: we hand-allocate every on- ... buffer and choose its pipeline depth (e.g. triple-buffered K/V so the load warp runs ahead), alias TMEM buffers with non-overlapping lifetimes (QK scores, P, and the softmax statistics share one allocation ... PV accumulator keeps its own), hand data between warps ... explicit producer/consumer barriers for a deterministic pipeline, and make both passes persistent — one CTA per SM looping over tiles. None of this is expressible in plain Triton, and the persistent structure in particular gives us a place to make our own scheduling decisions — the foundation for §2.2.
...
We found them with a consistent methodology: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU) to read hardware counters such as tensor-core/TMEM pipeline utilization, SM-busy, and register spills (which show up as local-memory traffic); the ptxas dump logs to confirm spills; and TritonBench in profiler-measure mode for clean before/after A/B latency. The optimizations fall into two groups. Some we adopt from the FA4 implementation — which itself shows that TLX can express, in readable Python, the same techniques a hand-written CuteDSL kernel uses. Others we derive ourselves, from profiling and analysis of our own kernel, targeting the jagged broadcast-Q workload specifically.
...
- Scheduling jagged tiles across SMs — software load balancing plus Cluster Launch Control keep every SM busy despite the order-of-magnitude length skew of jagged inputs (forward and backward).
- Multi-stage dQ staging — a double-buffered SMEM staging pipeline hides the heavily contended broadcast-Q dQ reduce-add, the #1 backward bottleneck.
- Early tensor-memory release — freeing the dQ tensor-memory buffer before its final stores lets the MMA warp start the next tile’s dQ matmul sooner.
- Loop peeling — splitting the KV loop into a branch-free bulk pass and a tiny masked tail removes per-iteration mask overhead and the register spills it causes.
- 2-CTA collaborative MMA — two CTAs cooperate on a single matmul to raise tensor-core utilization in the matmul-heavy backward (adopted from FA4).

The backward is matmul-heavy — computing dQ, dK, and dV takes five GEMMs per K/V block — and a single CTA does not fully utilize the Blackwell tensor cores on its own. We adopt FA4’s 2-CTA (paired-CTA tcgen05) scheme: two CTAs in a cluster cooperate on one wider collaborative matmul over two adjacent K/V blocks of the same (batch, head), splitting the accumulator rows across the two SMs and exchanging the dS intermediate on-chip over distributed shared memory (DSMEM) rather than through global memory. The structural changes — warp specialization, persistent execution, explicit SMEM/TMEM allocation with reuse aliasing, and barrier-mediated pipelining — set the stage, and the optimizations layered on top — software load balancing, Cluster Launch Control, multi-stage dQ staging, early TMEM release, loop peeling, and 2-CTA collaborative MMA — recovered most of the remaining headroom. Together they let the TLX kernel match or beat FA4 on both passes for the production jagged shapes, while retaining full broadcast-Q, sliding-window, and GQA support.

Beyond raw performance, the biggest win is development efficiency. Much of the low-level plumbing that CuteDSL writes by hand — async pipelines, barrier management, tcgen05 MMA setup — is instead handled by the TLX compiler, so we express intent rather than machinery, in a fraction of the code. That leverage lets the team prototype, profile, and land every optimization above quickly, and then fork the same kernel into MXFP8 and block-sparse variants with little extra code. signals.title: Eight-Bit LLM Training Now Matches Full Precision: MIT and NVIDIA Fix Root Cause
signals.excerpt:
Researchers from MIT and Carnegie Mellon University have formally identified and corrected the mathematical root cause behind the residual accuracy gap that has kept native 8-bit floating-point training from matching full-precision results in large language models — a barrier that, if the method holds at production scale, would allow every organization running frontier LLM pre-training to use the 2× arithmetic throughput of FP8 hardware without any quality penalty.
...
Modern AI hardware ships with dedicated FP8 compute units that deliver twice the arithmetic throughput of the 16-bit brain float (BF16) operations that currently dominate production training. On NVIDIA's H100, FP8 tensor cores reach 3,958 teraflops with sparsity versus 1,979 teraflops for BF16. In principle, a fully native FP8 training pipeline could halve hardware requirements or double effective batch sizes without adding a single GPU — at a time when frontier model pre-training runs routinely cost tens of millions of dollars.

The problem has always been in the attention mechanism. Linear layers adapt reasonably well to lower precision; the softmax-based attention core does not. Production training pipelines have addressed this through hybrid strategies: running the forward pass in FP8 while falling back to BF16 or FP32 for sensitive backward-pass operations. NVIDIA's cuDNN and Transformer Engine, the standard production tools for FP8 training, follow this hybrid pattern. Those hybrid methods narrow the accuracy gap but have never fully closed it.

The paper posted to arXiv on September 29 — titled Delta-Matching: Closing the Final Gap of Native 8-bit Training for LLMs — identifies the root cause of that residual gap with a formal mathematical proof.
...

...
Rather than proposing another hybrid workaround, the authors derive a closed-form correction. Delta-Matching adjusts the stale scaling factor δˢᵗᵃˡᵉ = ⟨dOᵢ, Ôᵢ⟩ — the term that becomes inconsistent when forward and backward operands quantize independently under different scaling factors — so that the softmax gradient zero-row-sum invariant is exactly restored.

The fix operates at the level of block-scaled FP8 matrix multiplications. Both the forward pass and backward pass of every attention-core operation — the Q·Kᵀ product, the P·V product, and their backward-pass transposes — run natively in FP8 without requiring any demotion to BF16. The FP8 format asymmetry is addressed directly: E4M3 format (four exponent bits, three mantissa bits), which provides finer precision and is used in the forward pass, and E5M2 format (five exponent bits, two mantissa bits), which provides wider dynamic range and is used in the backward pass, are reconciled so their respective scaling factors remain consistent across the forward-backward boundary.

Practically, Delta-Matching requires no architectural changes, no reduced global batch size, and no auxiliary forward-pass outputs that some competing methods depend on. The authors describe it as a compatible drop-in training improvement to existing pipelines.

The difference from prior hybrid methods is specific and quantitative. NVIDIA's cuDNN/Transformer Engine hybrid, the industry standard, reaches a validation cross-entropy of 1.6105 on the authors' benchmark — better than naive FP8 at 1.8970, but still materially below the BF16 baseline of 1.4178. Delta-Matching training loss and downstream benchmark performance are reported to match the BF16/FP32 mixed-precision baseline across all tested scales: 569 million, 1.67 billion, and 5.29 billion parameters.
...
Song Han's group has produced a series of influential quantization methods for large language models over the past several years. SmoothQuant, a training-free 8-bit quantization method, is integrated into NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM production inference stack. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) won the Best Paper award at MLSys 2024. Both are inference-time methods that quantize a trained model's weights for efficient deployment; they assume a fully trained, full-precision model as their input.

COAT (Compressing Optimizer states and Activations for memory-efficient Training), published at ICLR 2025, extended the lab's work into the training phase itself — achieving a 1.54× memory and 1.43× speedup on the OLMo-1B and OLMo-7B models by compressing optimizer states and activations. COAT addresses how much memory a training run consumes; it does not address the attention backward-pass numerical accuracy problem that Delta-Matching solves. The two methods are orthogonal.
...
Delta-Matching's path may be considerably shorter. Song Han co-founded DeePhi Technology, an inference-optimization startup acquired by Xilinx in 2018 (since absorbed into AMD). He later co-founded OmniML, an AI efficiency company acquired by NVIDIA in 2023. Han Cai is now on staff at NVIDIA Research. NVIDIA already ships SmoothQuant and AWQ — both from the same lab — in TensorRT-LLM's production inference stack.

That combination — authors with active NVIDIA Research affiliations, a lab with two methods already in NVIDIA's production stack, and a paper that specifically benchmarks its method against NVIDIA's own cuDNN/Transformer Engine hybrid and characterizes it as the correction to the residual gap that hybrid leaves — means Delta-Matching has an unusually direct institutional pathway from preprint to integration into the hardware that runs most frontier model training.
...

It does not require QK normalization, NoPE (no positional encoding), changes to global batch size, or the auxiliary forward-pass outputs that some prior memory-efficient FP8 methods depend on. The authors describe it as a compatible plug-in training upgrade to existing pipelines, applicable to standard transformer architectures without modifying the model definition or retuning learning rates.

The authors have not announced a timeline, but the institutional context suggests a faster-than-typical path. Both Song Han and Han Cai hold active affiliations at NVIDIA Research, and NVIDIA has already integrated two prior methods from the same lab — SmoothQuant and AWQ — into TensorRT-LLM. The paper explicitly benchmarks Delta-Matching against the cuDNN/Transformer Engine hybrid that NVIDIA ships today and frames Delta-Matching as a correction to the gap that hybrid leaves. Code, trained checkpoints, and data recipes are described in the paper as forthcoming. Independent replication at frontier model scale — tens to hundreds of billions of parameters — will likely be the key technical gate before any production framework integration.
...
SmoothQuant, AWQ, and COAT address different parts of the LLM efficiency problem. SmoothQuant and AWQ are post-training quantization methods: they take a fully trained, full-precision model and compress its weights for faster, cheaper inference deployment. COAT is a training-time method that compresses optimizer states and activations to reduce the peak memory footprint of a training run. None of these methods touch the backward-pass numerical accuracy of the attention core. The stale-delta problem is a training-time accuracy problem — it corrupts the gradients computed during backpropagation through the attention mechanism, causing the model that emerges from training to fall short of what full-precision training would have produced. Delta-Matching corrects that specific error; the four methods address complementary rather than competing problems.

The benchmark, conducted by ServeTheHome's Patrick Kennedy at an F5 lab in California and sponsored by F5, ran Qwen3-32B in FP8 precision on Supermicro servers with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs each, and measured P90 latency across 60-minute runs at varying concurrency levels.

The throughput gap emerged specifically when the cluster's KV cache — the GPU memory region that stores intermediate attention computations for active inference sessions — ran oversubscribed: at 200 concurrent requests each carrying 20,000 input tokens, the cluster was running at 1.24 times capacity. Under those conditions, F5's BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes (BNK), running on the DPU, outpaced the host-CPU-based Envoy AI Gateway by more than three to one. At lighter loads — 150 concurrent requests at 10,000 input tokens each — the two solutions performed comparably, which means the 3.24x figure is not a headline number for all deployments, but a ceiling that applies specifically to oversubscribed, high-concurrency inference workloads.

The core architectural innovation in BNK's Endpoint Picker (EPP) is not that it runs on a DPU. It is that it reads live NVIDIA NIM telemetry and routes each incoming inference request to the GPU most likely to have both the available capacity and the relevant cached context for that request.
...
A gateway that does not read KV-cache state routes requests blindly — potentially sending a request to a GPU whose cache contains none of the relevant prefix, guaranteeing a cache miss. BNK's EPP, by contrast, queries NVIDIA NIM statistics continuously and steers each request to the GPU most likely to service it without a cache miss. This is why the performance advantage widens as load increases: at 150 concurrent × 10,000-token requests, there is enough headroom that cache misses are rare regardless of routing strategy. At 200 concurrent × 20,000-token requests — 1.24 times KV-cache capacity — the difference between cache-aware and cache-blind routing becomes the dominant factor in throughput.

One critical constraint: this benefit is conditional on NVIDIA NIM telemetry. BNK's EPP receives the GPU metrics it needs to make intelligent routing decisions because NVIDIA NIM exposes them. signals.excerpt:
Janus: Cross-Vendor Vulkan GGUF Inference Without Python

# Janus Brings Vulkan GGUF Inference to AMD and Intel GPUs Without Python or Docker

 By Jaxson Reed October 2, 2026 

Deploying local large language models on consumer hardware usually requires choosing between heavy runtime abstractions. Users either pull multi-gigabyte container layers with Docker and Ollama, or assemble fragile Python virtual environments with PyTorch and vendor-specific accelerator wheels. For systems running AMD Radeon or Intel Arc graphics, that setup is compounded by fractured software stacks: AMD’s ROCm provides uneven support across consumer RDNA architectures, while Intel’s SYCL toolchains require substantial oneAPI runtime packages.

The newly released open-source project Janus tackles this deployment friction by packaging local inference into a standalone Go binary. By coupling an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server (`/v1/chat/completions`) directly to `llama.cpp`’s Vulkan compute backend via dynamic library bindings, Janus executes `.gguf` quantized models across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs out of the box.

The tool provides model hot-swapping (`POST /models/load`), GGUF chat template auto-detection, and native ` ` tag token splitting for reasoning models, while bypassing Python, Docker, and container daemons entirely.
...
The core architectural choice behind Janus is standardizing on the Vulkan compute API instead of proprietary accelerator runtimes. In high-performance enterprise datacenters, proprietary toolchains dominate: NVIDIA relies on CUDA and cuBLAS, while enterprise deployments on AMD Instinct accelerators leverage ROCm and HIP.

On consumer desktops and homelabs, however, proprietary frameworks create severe compatibility hurdles. AMD’s official ROCm releases historically prioritize Linux and data-center CDNA hardware, leaving Windows desktop Radeon users to wrestle with community ports or experimental drivers. Intel Arc discrete GPUs and Core Ultra mobile chips require Intel’s SYCL/oneAPI runtime, creating a fragmented maintenance matrix for multi-machine homelabs.

Vulkan compute levels this playing field. Because Vulkan is a cross-platform graphics and compute standard maintained by Khronos, modern GPU drivers from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel ship native SPIR-V shader execution pipelines by default. By binding to pre-compiled `llama.cpp` Vulkan dynamic link libraries (`llama.dll` on Windows, `libllama.so` on Linux), Janus allows an Intel Arc A770, an AMD Radeon RX 7800 XT, or an NVIDIA GeForce card to execute the exact same binary without installing developer toolkits or kernel modules.

| Stack Component | Standard PyTorch / Ollama | Janus (Go + Vulkan) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime Dependencies | Docker daemon, Python 3.10+, CUDA/ROCm runtimes (2–15 GB) | Standalone executable + llama.dll (~50 MB total) |
| Hardware Compatibility | Vendor-specific builds (CUDA for NV, ROCm for AMD, SYCL for Intel) | Universal cross-vendor execution via standard Vulkan drivers |
| Model Loading & Hot-Swap | CLI restart or internal container orchestration | In-process hot-swap via HTTP endpoint (`POST /models/load`) |
| Prefill / GEMM Tuning | Highly tuned assembly micro-kernels (cuBLAS, rocBLAS) | Generic SPIR-V shaders; 5–20% lower prefill compute efficiency |
...
For users running quantized models on modern APUs—such as the memory configurations we examined in our analysis of unified memory architectures and 120B MoE models—Vulkan delivers sustained memory saturation without requiring vendor software suites.
...
Janus does not aim to replace high-throughput enterprise inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, which specialize in multi-tenant batching, continuous PagedAttention scheduling, and distributed tensor parallelism.

Instead, Janus fills a clear operational void: providing a zero-overhead, 50-megabyte OpenAI-compatible bridge for desktop machines and workstations. By discarding the multi-gigabyte bloat of Python environments and container engines in favor of native Go and cross-platform Vulkan shaders, it offers AMD and Intel GPU owners a dependable, low-friction entry point for local model serving.

signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA has open-sourced OSMO, a Kubernetes-native workflow orchestrator the company built internally to manage the sprawling compute demands of its robotics AI programs, including Project GR00T, Isaac Lab, and Isaac Sim. The tool lets robotics teams define training, simulation, and hardware-in-the-loop tasks in a single YAML file, then automatically routes those jobs to the right tier of compute, from massive GB200 data center clusters down to compact Jetson AGX Thor edge devices. The release, part of an unusually active week for developer infrastructure open-sourcing, arrives alongside Cloudflare's Forge code-generation pipeline and new agent frameworks from AWS, Microsoft, WSO2, and OpenAI. For an industry racing to build physical AI systems, OSMO addresses a problem that has quietly throttled progress: orchestrating workloads across wildly different hardware without writing custom infrastructure code for every project.

The release lands at a moment when robotics and physical AI have become one of the most capital-intensive and infrastructure-hungry corners of the technology industry, with humanoid robots moving from demo stages to factory floors and simulation increasingly standing in for scarce real ... world training data. NVIDIA's decision to give away a tool it built for its own flagship robotics projects signals a strategic bet: the company would rather set the orchestration standard that the rest of the robotics industry builds on top of, extending its dominance from chips and simulation software into the workflow layer that ties everything together. It also reflects a broader pattern this week, ... which major infrastructure providers, from Cloudflare to AWS to Microsoft, chose to open-source tooling rather than keep it proprietary, a sign that platform companies increasingly see developer adoption, not licensing fees, as the real prize.
...
At its core, OSMO is a workflow orchestrator built on Kubernetes, the dominant system for managing containerized applications at scale. What sets it apart from generic Kubernetes tooling is its specific focus on the robotics development lifecycle, which typically spans several distinct compute environments: large-scale training on data center GPUs, physics simulation on dedicated clusters, and final validation on the actual embedded hardware that will ship inside a robot.

Historically, moving a job between these environments required robotics engineers to write custom infrastructure code tailored to each compute tier, a process NVIDIA says consumed significant engineering time that could otherwise go toward the actual AI models. OSMO collapses that complexity into a single YAML configuration file, letting a developer describe a training job, a simulation run, or a hardware-in-the-loop test once and have the orchestrator figure out where and how to run it, whether that destination is a GB200 cluster in a data center or a Jetson AGX Thor module embedded in a robot.

NVIDIA has used OSMO internally across three of its most prominent robotics initiatives: Project GR00T, its foundation model effort for humanoid robots; Isaac Lab, its reinforcement learning framework; and Isaac Sim, its simulation platform built on Omniverse. The fact that NVIDIA trusted OSMO to manage workflows across all three suggests the tool has already been stress-tested against the kind of production complexity that smaller robotics startups are only now beginning to encounter.
...
Open-sourcing an internal orchestration tool is a calculated move rather than a charitable one. By releasing OSMO publicly, NVIDIA positions itself as the default infrastructure layer for an entire generation of robotics companies that are building on its GPUs, its Isaac simulation tools, and now, potentially, its workflow orchestration as well. Every robotics team that adopts OSMO becomes more deeply embedded in NVIDIA's ecosystem, reinforcing the company's position at nearly every layer of the physical AI stack, from silicon to software.
...
OSMO's release did not happen in isolation. Cloudflare simultaneously open-sourced Forge, a code generation pipeline designed to automatically produce SDKs, CLIs, and documentation, a tool aimed squarely at reducing the manual maintenance burden that platform companies face as their APIs multiply. AWS, for its part, released Strands Harness on September 21, an open-source agent framework capable of running locally or across any cloud environment, explicitly designed to avoid locking developers into AWS infrastructure alone.

Microsoft shipped version 1.19.0 of its Agent Framework on September 18, stabilizing Python AG-UI hosting and adding workflow recovery capabilities, while WSO2 reached general availability for Agent Manager on September 15, an open-source control plane for governing AI agents across different frameworks, models, and deployment targets. OpenAI rounded out the month by launching its Agents API in public beta on September 10, exposing the orchestration infrastructure that powers its own Codex product to outside developers.
...
these releases describe an industry- ... shift in strategy. ... than compete purely on proprietary platforms, major ... providers are racing to open-source the control planes, orchestrators, and frameworks that sit underneath AI applications, essentially competing to become the substrate that everyone else builds on. For robotics specifically, OSMO's arrival suggests that the chaotic, bespoke infrastructure practices that have characterized early robotics AI development may be consolidating around a small number of standardized, NVIDIA-adjacent tools.
...
For engineering teams building robotics products, OSMO's open-source release lowers a real barrier to entry. Smaller robotics startups, which often lack the dedicated infrastructure engineering teams that a company like NVIDIA can deploy, have historically struggled to build the orchestration layer needed to move seamlessly between simulation and physical testing. A freely available, battle-tested tool addresses that gap directly, potentially accelerating the pace at which smaller players can iterate on humanoid robots, industrial automation systems, and other physical AI products.
...
There are tradeoffs worth watching, however. Adopting OSMO means building workflows around a tool deeply tied to NVIDIA's own hardware and software stack, including GB200 clusters and Jetson devices, which could deepen dependency on a single vendor even as it solves an immediate engineering problem. Competing chipmakers and cloud providers will likely need to respond with their own orchestration offerings or interoperability layers to avoid ceding this part of the stack entirely to NVIDIA.

Still, for an industry grappling with the operational complexity of training and deploying physical AI systems at scale, a standardized, open-source orchestrator addressing the simulation-to-hardware pipeline fills a genuine gap in the current tooling landscape. As more robotics companies move from pilot programs to full production deployment, the tools that manage that transition, quietly and without much public fanfare, may end up mattering as much as the headline-grabbing models and chips themselves.

# AgentScope 2.0：可审计、可追踪的RAG as Service智能体操作系统

 AgentScope 2.0：可审计、可追踪的RAG as Service智能体操作系统 

### 1. 这不是又一个LLM框架，而是一套“可拆解、可追踪、可审计”的智能体工程操作系统

AgentScope——这个名字最近在技术圈里出现的频率，已经快赶上当年Docker刚火起来那会儿。但和当年大家一窝蜂学Dockerfile不同，这次很多人点开GitHub仓库后第一反应是：“这文档怎么全是英文？中文资料在哪？”“Java版到底支不支持？是不是只给Python用？”“RAG as Service这个新提法，到底是包装概念还是真有东西？”——这些不是小白疑问，而是真实落地团队在评估技术选型时最朴素的三连问。
...
核心关键词就三个： AgentScope、RAG as Service、AgentScope 2.0。它们不是并列关系，而是演进链条——1.0解决“能不能跑”，2.0解决“敢不敢上生产”，而RAG as Service则是2.0里真正把抽象能力拉回地面的关键落点。如果你正在为大模型应用陷入“Prompt调参疲劳”“Agent状态不可见”“多跳推理结果无法归因”这些问题头疼，那AgentScope不是锦上添花，而是手术刀级别的工具。它不承诺“一键生成商业级Agent”，但能让你在三天内，把一个混沌的LLM调用链，变成一张可标注、可回溯、可压测的拓扑图。适合两类人：一类是带团队做AI产品落地的技术负责人，需要快速建立可控的Agent交付流水线；另一类是独立开发者或研究员，想摆脱LangChain那种“写十行代码，debug两小时”的碎片化体验，真正把Agent当成一个可部署、可监控、可版本管理的软件单元来对待。
...
第三，状态必须可审计、可回溯。 AgentScope 2.0引入`RunRecord`机制，每个Agent执行周期自动生成结构化日志，包含：输入Message ID、调用模型名称及Token数、输出Message ID、耗时、异常堆栈（如有）、关联的Trace ID。这些记录默认存入本地`run_records.db`，也可对接ELK或OpenTelemetry。关键在于，`RunRecord`不是事后日志，而是执行过程中的第一等公民——你可以用`record.get_input()`拿到原始输入，用`record.get_output()`拿到结构化输出，甚至用`record.get_sub_calls()`查看它内部调用了哪些子Agent。我们曾用这套机制定位到一个隐蔽Bug：某个Agent在处理长文本时，因LLM返回格式不稳定，导致后续Agent解析JSON失败。通过查询`RunRecord`中`output.content`字段的分布，发现23%的响应开头多了个不可见的Unicode字符`\u200b`，问题根源瞬间清晰。

第四，RAG必须作为一级服务而非插件。 这是AgentScope 2.0最颠覆性的升级。传统RAG方案（如LlamaIndex）把检索、重排序、提示构造全塞进一个`Retriever`类里，调试时像在黑盒里摸大象。AgentScope则将RAG拆解为标准服务：`RetrievalService`负责向向量库发起查询，`RerankService`负责对结果重排序，`PromptService`负责组装最终Prompt。三者通过统一的`RAGRequest`/`RAGResponse` Schema通信，且每个服务都可独立替换——你可以用FAISS换Milvus，用BGE-reranker换Cohere，甚至把`PromptService`换成一个调用外部API的微服务。更重要的是，这些服务调用同样生成`RunRecord`，和普通Agent完全平权。我们上线后，RAG模块的平均调试时间从4.2小时降到27分钟，因为问题能精准定位到是检索召回率低，还是重排序阈值设错，而不是笼统地说“RAG效果不好”。
...
Layer 3：Service Layer（服务层） 这就是2.0新增的RAG as Service核心。`RetrievalService`抽象出`search()`方法，`RerankService`抽象出`rerank()`方法，`PromptService`抽象出`build_prompt()`方法。所有服务都遵循`ServiceConfig`配置范式，支持YAML文件热加载。我们把向量库连接参数、重排序模型路径、Prompt模板都写进`rag_config.yaml`，运维同学改配置不用动代码，改完`agent_scope reload_service`命令即可生效。
...
先破除一个广泛误解： AgentScope官方确实没有发布Java SDK，但这不等于Java项目不能用。我们团队的工业诊断系统就是Java Spring Boot架构，解决方案很务实：用Python启动AgentScope Runtime作为独立服务，Java后端通过HTTP API与其交互。AgentScope 2.0内置了`FastAPI`服务端，暴露`/v1/agents/{agent_id}/run`和`/v1/orchestrators/{workflow_id}/run`两个核心Endpoint。Java端只需用`RestTemplate`或`WebClient`调用，传入标准JSON Message，接收标准JSON Response。我们封装了一个`AgentScopeClient`工具类，120行代码搞定所有交互，比引入任何Java版LLM框架都轻量。

signals.excerpt:
Not every step in an AI agent needs a model that writes. Many steps only need a model that picks. That is the idea behind Strands Decider 2B, a new open-source release from Amazon Web Services' Strands Labs team. AWS describes it as a lightweight "decision model" built to make fast choices inside agentic workflows without generating any text.

The model is out now on Hugging Face. The full codebase, training scripts and examples are on GitHub. AWS has tuned it for local use and quick experiments, so developers can run it on their own laptops as well as in public cloud environments.
...
AWS says decision models are not new, but they drew little attention until recently. That changed a couple of weeks ago, when a startup called TypeSafe AI Inc. released Jev. Jev was designed to make fast, structured decisions that software and AI agents can use directly.

AWS credits Jev with showing how useful this class of model can be. It also says Jev has structural weaknesses. The main one, in AWS's view, is a parallel output structure that causes performance problems when the model has to handle intricate reasoning. Strands Decider 2B is the company's first serious attempt to improve on the concept.
...
The model starts from a standard LLM. AWS took the base torso of Qwen3.5-2B and removed the ... "LLM head," the ... produces text. In ... with roughly
...
The team then fine-tuned the Qwen3.5-2B torso with a rank-16 LoRA adapter. LoRA is a common technique that adapts a model by training a small set of added weights rather than the whole ... . Here, it teaches the model to score the hidden ... of the available choices directly
...
AWS says it went through many iterations before this release. The 2-billion-parameter size was a deliberate choice. According to the company, it is small enough to run on a local machine with latency under 150 milliseconds, but still capable enough to handle complex decisions. If you have been following smaller models running on local hardware, the Qwen base will be familiar.

On benchmarks, AWS reports that Strands Decider 2B scored highly on accuracy and calibration on JevBench, compared with other open-source models of the same 2B size. Calibration measures how well a model's confidence matches how often it is actually right. For a model whose confidence score is its only form of explanation, that is the number to watch.
...
AWS lists several tasks where it expects the model to help:

- Model routing: sending a request to the right model.
- Tool selection: choosing which tool an agent should call.
- Context management: deciding what information to keep or pass along.
- Guardrail enforcement: checking whether an action should be allowed.
- Policy classification: sorting inputs against defined rules.

The company also sees the release as a step toward "hybrid agents." In that setup, a decision model handles simple, repetitive choices, and an LLM takes over when a problem needs real reasoning. AWS says its broader goal is to speed up agentic AI development across the developer community.
...
This release suggests that agent builders are starting to break their systems into specialized parts, not route every step through one large model. Many agent steps are really multiple-choice questions: which tool, which model, allow or block. Using a full LLM for those is slow and expensive. A small model that answers in under 150 milliseconds could change the economics, which fits a wider push toward cheaper models that come close to flagship performance.
...
Several things are worth watching. Will independent tests confirm AWS's JevBench results? How will TypeSafe AI respond with future versions of Jev? And will hybrid agents become a common pattern, or stay a niche optimization? The open release means developers can find out for themselves.

candidates.topic: Auditable and traceable AI agents for production
candidates.angle: AgentScope 2.0 introduces 'RAG as Service' to make AI agent workflows auditable, traceable, and debuggable, bridging the gap from 'can it run?' to 'can it run reliably in production?' by tackling issues like agent state visibility and result attribution in multi-hop reasoning.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers struggle to debug, monitor, and ensure reliability for AI agents in production environments, where agent actions often remain a 'black box' and multi-step reasoning failures are hard to pinpoint.
candidates.why_now: The latest release of AgentScope 2.0, with its focus on auditable and traceable agent systems via 'RAG as Service,' directly responds to the growing need for production-grade agentic applications that can be reliably deployed and maintained.
candidates.hook_seed: Agent failures? See the whole trace.

candidates.angle: Researchers from MIT and Carnegie Mellon University, with NVIDIA, have formally identified and corrected the mathematical root cause behind the residual accuracy gap that has kept native 8-bit floating-point training from matching full-precision results in large language models. This breakthrough could allow every organization running frontier LLM pre-training to use the 2x throughput of FP8 hardware without any quality penalty.
candidates.audience_pain: Organizations developing and pre-training large language models face a dilemma: choose faster 8-bit training with a potential accuracy trade-off, or slower 16-bit training for full precision.
candidates.why_now: This significant research breakthrough eliminates a critical barrier, allowing developers to leverage the 2x arithmetic throughput of FP8 hardware for LLM training without compromising model quality, fundamentally shifting the economics and speed of pre-training.

candidates.topic: Cross-vendor GGUF inference for AMD/Intel GPUs
candidates.angle: Janus, a new open-source project, enables cross-vendor Vulkan GGUF inference on AMD Radeon and Intel Arc GPUs without requiring Python or Docker, simplifying local LLM deployment and overcoming fragmented software stacks.
candidates.audience_pain: Many developers are constrained by NVIDIA-centric AI ecosystems and face significant hurdles trying to run LLMs locally on their AMD Radeon or Intel Arc GPUs due to complex software setups.
candidates.why_now: The release of Janus directly addresses a long-standing pain point for non-NVIDIA GPU owners, making local LLM inference more accessible and removing typical deployment friction (Python/Docker).

candidates.topic: Auto-tuned kernels for vLLM inference speedups
candidates.angle: PyTorch researchers integrated Helion into vLLM's linear backend, reporting 1.11x to 1.18x GEMM speedups on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. This approach turns GEMM variant selection into a tunable parameter instead of relying on hand-written dispatch heuristics, simplifying kernel implementation while boosting performance.
candidates.audience_pain: Optimizing LLM inference performance, particularly with widely used serving frameworks like vLLM, often requires deep expertise in low-level kernel tuning or relies on static, less efficient dispatch heuristics.
candidates.why_now: New research demonstrating 1.11x-1.18x speedups for vLLM on Hopper GPUs through auto-tuned kernels provides a practical, performance-enhancing solution for developers looking to optimize their LLM serving infrastructure without custom kernel development.

candidates.topic: Local LLM deployment simplified with ds4
candidates.angle: Salvatore Sanfilippo, the creator of Redis, launched `ds4`, a new minimalist tool specifically designed for running LLMs locally, offering a lightweight alternative to complex Docker setups or fragile Python virtual environments.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers struggle with the complexity and overhead of setting up local LLM inference environments using Docker or managing Python virtual environments with numerous dependencies.
candidates.why_now: The recent launch of `ds4` from a highly credible and respected figure (Redis creator) has garnered significant community attention (Hacker News), indicating strong demand for simpler local LLM solutions.
candidates.hook_seed: Run LLMs locally. No Docker, no Python.

candidates.topic: Robust agentic RAG for enterprise knowledge
candidates.angle: New agentic RAG frameworks like Tencent's WeKnora and Progress Agentic RAG offer robust solutions for enterprises, unifying diverse knowledge sources (Notion, SharePoint, local files), supporting multi-step reasoning, and providing verifiable answers via 'shared Agentic Knowledge Layers' for complex business workflows.
candidates.audience_pain: Enterprises struggle to implement reliable RAG solutions that can integrate disparate internal knowledge sources and support complex, multi-step reasoning with verifiable outputs for business-critical applications.
candidates.why_now: The simultaneous emergence of frameworks like Tencent's open-source WeKnora and Progress Agentic RAG signals a clear market demand and growing maturity in comprehensive, agent-powered RAG solutions designed for enterprise scale and complexity.

candidates.angle: EntroPack compresses neural weights at finely adjustable storage rates, combining lattice quantization, sampled rate estimation, and tiled GPU decoding to meet target bitrates without calibration or fine-tuning, thus significantly reducing memory footprint and storage for large models.
candidates.audience_pain: Deploying large language models often hits memory and storage limits on hardware, and existing compression methods offer coarse adjustments or require extensive fine-tuning.
candidates.why_now: The introduction of EntroPack provides a novel, precise method for neural weight compression, allowing developers to target specific bitrates without complex calibration, directly addressing the practical challenge of making large models fit into resource-constrained environments.

candidates.topic: Serverless and reserved serving for open LLMs
candidates.angle: Prime Intellect launched Prime Inference, a serverless and reserved-capacity serving platform for frontier open-source models, reporting high throughput and nearly 40% lower p90 inter-token latency due to prefill/decode disaggregation on Blackwell GPUs.
candidates.audience_pain: Deploying and scaling open-source LLMs in production efficiently, managing infrastructure costs, and achieving consistently low inference latency are significant challenges for developers.
candidates.why_now: The launch of Prime Inference provides a specialized, high-performance serving solution that directly addresses the pain points of scaling open-source LLMs, offering both serverless flexibility and reserved capacity options with demonstrated latency improvements on cutting-edge hardware like Blackwell GPUs.
candidates.hook_seed: Serve open LLMs. Serverless, low latency.

candidates.topic: Open-source infrastructure for scalable MoE training
candidates.angle: AllenAI's Olmo-core 3 is a significant upgrade to their open-source framework, enabling scalable Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM training up to the trillion-parameter range while preserving computational efficiency, bridging the gap between dense and MoE models.
candidates.audience_pain: Training extremely large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models efficiently presents significant infrastructure and scaling challenges, often requiring custom solutions or immense resources.
candidates.why_now: The release of Olmo-core 3 provides an open-source, scalable framework specifically designed to tackle the complexities of trillion-parameter MoE training, making advanced model architectures more accessible for researchers and large-scale model builders.
candidates.hook_seed: Trillion-parameter MoEs? Open source does it.

candidates.angle: F5 benchmarks show that running their AI-aware load balancer natively on NVIDIA BlueField-3 Data Processing Units (DPUs) delivered a 3.24x throughput advantage over Envoy AI Gateway at peak concurrency, while freeing host CPU cores for other tasks, optimizing KV-cache-aware routing for H100s.
candidates.audience_pain: Achieving high throughput and efficient resource utilization for AI inference serving, especially at peak concurrency, remains a challenge, with network overhead and CPU contention often acting as bottlenecks.
candidates.why_now: Recent benchmarks definitively demonstrate how NVIDIA DPUs, combined with intelligent load balancing, can dramatically improve AI inference throughput (3.24x) by offloading routing and optimizing KV-cache management, offering a clear path to significant infrastructure efficiency gains.
